assessment.nobel_worthiness: A foundational, widely taught framework for how interest groups shape trade policy (the 'protection for sale' line of work). It changed how economists model political-economy constraints on policy, and the theory has since been tested empirically. Helpman and Grossman's wider joint research programme on innovation and growth in open economies adds weight beyond this entry's narrow description.
assessment.attribution: A clean two-person core with a long, stable collaboration. Helpman is also credited on B041, so any Helpman award would have to be weighed against that entry.
assessment.maturity: Very mature. The core work dates from the 1990s, and decades of use and testing support its durability.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would prefer to frame the award around growth-and-trade or around trade-politics.
The theory's empirical support is mixed, though influence is not in doubt.
Overlap with B041 on Helpman.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: High. Linking technology, tasks and trade exposure to labour demand and wage inequality is a central empirical question. The China-shock work used credible, shift-share, quasi-experimental local labour market designs, and the task-based view of skill demand reshaped the discussion of polarization. Policy and public influence are large.
assessment.attribution: Autor is the common thread across tasks, polarization and the China shock. Hanson is central to the trade-exposure work. Katz has long-running contributions on skill demand and wage structure, but the 'task' framework also draws on contributors outside this entry. Dorn is a real co-author whom a three-name cap leaves out.
assessment.maturity: Mature enough: 10-20 years of replication, critique and extension. The shift-share identification debate has been absorbed rather than overturned.
uncertainties: Credit for the task framework is shared with scholars outside the credited names.
Shift-share identification has been criticised, and the long-run magnitude of the shock is debated.
Katz also appears on B002.
The 2023 and 2024 prizes touched adjacent topics (labour market gender gaps, institutions and technology).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Kiyotaki-Moore credit-cycles model is a canonical account of how collateral constraints amplify and propagate shocks. It underlies much of modern macro-finance, including after the 2008 crisis. It is a clear theoretical contribution with a large downstream empirical and quantitative literature.
assessment.attribution: The 1997 paper makes the Kiyotaki-Moore pairing the cleanest. Gertler and Gilchrist's financial-accelerator work is complementary, and the 2022 prize (Bernanke, Diamond, Dybvig) already recognised neighbouring banking and crisis themes.
assessment.maturity: Very mature, with nearly three decades of influence.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize may reduce appetite.
Whether to include Gertler/Gilchrist and how to divide credit for the financial-accelerator line.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Large-scale administrative data was used to measure intergenerational mobility, neighbourhood effects and teacher value-added. This has changed both the evidence base and policy debate about opportunity. The methodological and data innovation and the credibility-revolution style of design are strong. Chetty's wider work on public economics is a further asset.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the clear leader, with Friedman and Hendren as principal collaborators on the mobility and neighbourhood-effects papers. Katz's role on Moving to Opportunity is real but more tied to B038 and to the experiment itself.
assessment.maturity: Moderate. The key results are roughly 10 years old. Replication and data-access issues and some debate about causal neighbourhood effects remain, but the core findings have held up.
uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the work mature enough.
Correlational mobility maps versus causal neighbourhood effects.
Credit division with Katz.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: HANK models integrate household heterogeneity and marginal propensities to consume into New Keynesian analysis. They changed how monetary and fiscal transmission is understood and are now standard in central banks and research. It is a significant conceptual and quantitative advance.
assessment.attribution: The Kaplan-Moll-Violante 2018 paper is the clear anchor, but the broader heterogeneous-agent macro tradition (Aiyagari, Bewley, Huggett, Krusell-Smith) is acknowledged as earlier, which complicates attribution.
assessment.maturity: Moderate. It is influential but only about a decade old, and the framework is still evolving.
uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers to wait.
Attribution relative to the earlier heterogeneous-agent literature.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework, with nominal rigidities, the Calvo pricing model, and its microfounded policy analysis, underpins modern monetary policy practice and teaching. The conceptual and practical impact is very large.
assessment.attribution: Hard. Many contributors are credited (eight), and the proposed names are a judgment call. Taylor, Christiano-Eichenbaum, Smets and others made major contributions, and some of the intellectual ancestry has already been recognised in earlier prizes (Phelps, Lucas, Kydland-Prescott).
assessment.maturity: Very mature, though the post-2008 and post-2021 inflation debates have both tested and reaffirmed the framework.
uncertainties: The attribution problem is severe given a maximum of three laureates.
Whether any three-person subset would be seen as fair.
Overlap with B012 on Gertler.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Reviving long-run top-income and wealth measurement from tax data has reshaped the field and public debate. The data-construction contribution is substantial. Some of the interpretative and theoretical claims on the wealth-income ratio and r>g are contested.
assessment.attribution: The Piketty-Saez top-incomes work is the core, and Zucman is central on offshore wealth and distributional national accounts. Atkinson, whose pioneering work is not in the credited names, has died.
assessment.maturity: Mature in measurement terms, but data-construction methodology (e.g. imputation and treatment of capital income) remains debated.
uncertainties: Contested measurement choices and conclusions.
Whether the committee would treat the contribution as primarily data work or as a research programme with a lasting analytical core.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The alternating-offers bargaining model gave a tractable, widely used non-cooperative foundation for bargaining. It is used throughout labour, industrial organisation, macro search models and political economy. The theory is elegant and has had very broad downstream use.
assessment.attribution: Rubinstein (1982) is the clear originator. Wolinsky joins on the market-bargaining extensions (Rubinstein-Wolinsky 1985 and the follow-ups). Binmore's contributions to the Nash programme and to the alternating-offers analysis are significant but secondary, so I leave him out, with some uncertainty.
assessment.maturity: Very mature, with over 40 years of use.
uncertainties: Recent game-theory and mechanism-design prizes (2007, 2020) may weigh against another theory award.
Credit allocation between Rubinstein and Binmore.
